scenes.text: In 1775, the United States tried to conquer Canada. In 1812, it tried again. And for almost a century, many Americans believed Canada would join them sooner or later. So why didn't it?

Stick, the reporter character with olive PRESS helmet and dark blue PRESS vest, stands on the right pointing at the map with a curious face.

scenes.text: To understand it, we have to go back to 1774, when Britain made a surprising deal with the French-speaking Catholics of Quebec. The Quebec Act let them keep their religion, their language and their laws.
scenes.prompt: A British officer stick figure in a red coat handing a rolled scroll with a red wax seal to a group of French Canadian stick figure villagers wearing knitted tuque caps, a small wooden church with a cross behind them, the year 1774 written in marker at the top.

scenes.text: So when the American Revolution began, most Quebecers had little reason to join it.
scenes.prompt: Left side: American rebel stick figures in blue coats waving and beckoning. Right side: French Canadian villagers in tuque caps shrugging with their arms crossed, not interested. A thin dashed border line between the two groups.

scenes.text: In late 1775, American armies marched north anyway. They captured Montreal, then attacked Quebec City in a snowstorm on the last night of the year. The attack failed, and General Richard Montgomery was killed.
scenes.prompt: Tall stone fortress walls of Quebec City on a cliff during a heavy blizzard at night, small blue-coated American stick soldiers struggling up through deep snow with ladders, red-coated defenders on top of the walls, swirling snowflakes, no blood.

scenes.text: The Americans even wrote an open invitation into their first constitution. Article Eleven of the Articles of Confederation said Canada could join the Union whenever it wanted. Canada never said yes.
scenes.prompt: An old parchment document with the words ARTICLE XI written large at the top, next to it a long table with thirteen chairs filled by blue stick figures and one empty chair with a small red maple leaf on its back.

scenes.text: After the war, tens of thousands of Loyalists, Americans who had stayed loyal to the British crown, fled north. They built new towns in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and what is now Ontario, and they did not want to be American.
scenes.prompt: A long line of stick figure families walking north with wagons, suitcases and a cow, crossing a dashed border line from a blue area into a red area, small new log cabins being built on the red side.

scenes.text: In 1812, the United States declared war on Britain and invaded Canada again. Thomas Jefferson said that taking it would be a mere matter of marching.
scenes.prompt: A confident column of blue-coated American stick soldiers marching to the right with a drum and a flag, toward a red area labeled CANADA, the year 1812 written in marker at the top, a gentleman stick figure in a tailcoat smiling and pointing the way.

scenes.text: It was not. One American army surrendered at Detroit, and another was crushed at Queenston Heights.
scenes.prompt: Blue-coated American stick soldiers raising a white flag next to a small wooden fort on a river, red-coated soldiers and Indigenous allies standing confidently in front of them, a cliff with a red flag in the background. No blood.

scenes.text: Both sides burned the other's capital. Americans burned York, today's Toronto, and in 1814 British troops set fire to Washington, including the White House.
scenes.prompt: The White House drawn in simple black marker with cartoon orange flames and grey smoke coming out of the windows, small red-coated stick soldiers walking away in the foreground, the year 1814 written in marker. No people hurt.

scenes.text: The war ended in a draw. The Treaty of Ghent handed back every inch of land. But in Canada, the war became a founding story: the time they stopped an invasion.
scenes.prompt: Two stick figure diplomats, one in a blue coat and one in a red coat, shaking hands over a signed treaty on a small table, behind them a simple map of North America where the border has not changed, a small red maple leaf shining proudly.

scenes.text: The pressure didn't stop. Americans talked about Manifest Destiny, the idea that the United States should rule the whole continent. In 1846, the two sides nearly went to war over Oregon, before splitting it along the forty-ninth parallel.
scenes.prompt: A simple map of the western part of North America with a long straight dashed line drawn across it labeled 49, the area below colored light blue, the area above colored light red, a blue stick figure and a red stick figure each pulling one side of the map like a rope.

scenes.text: Then came the American Civil War, which built the largest army in North America, and raids into Canada by Irish-American veterans known as the Fenians.
scenes.prompt: Night scene at a river border: a small group of stick figure raiders in green caps crossing the river in a rowing boat toward red-coated Canadian militia stick figures waiting on the shore with lanterns.

scenes.text: Fear of their giant neighbour pushed the British colonies to unite. On July the first, 1867, Canada was born as one country.
scenes.prompt: Four stick figures representing provinces holding hands in a circle around a red map of Canada, fireworks above them, the year 1867 written in big marker numbers, a happy celebratory mood.

scenes.text: That same year, the United States bought Alaska from Russia, squeezing Canada from both sides. But Canada was now strong enough to stand on its own.
scenes.prompt: Map of North America: Alaska and the United States colored light blue on both sides of a red Canada, two blue arrows pressing inward, and a small red stick figure holding up a shield with a maple leaf in the middle of Canada, standing firm.

scenes.text: So the real reason Canada never became American comes down to four things. Quebec was kept loyal. The Loyalists fled north. Two invasions failed. And the threat itself pushed Canadians together.
